summary: This work investigates phase noise effects on superconducting qubit fidelity through time-domain numerical simulations with Qiskit-Dynamics, resolving a previous misinterpretation that claimed high-frequency noise components dominate fidelity loss. The authors demonstrate that noise components near the Rabi frequency and low-frequency components with large amplitude are the primary fidelity degradation sources, with high-frequency noise contributing only marginally through residual amplitude modulation.
motivation: As qubit coherence times and readout fidelities improve, phase noise in control signals becomes a critical limiting factor for achieving high-fidelity gates in complex pulse sequences. Prior work using filter-function formalism incorrectly concluded that high-frequency spectral components dominate fidelity loss, which the authors show stems from a misinterpretation of the phase-to-frequency noise PSD conversion.
method: The authors generated colored phase noise realizations with specified power spectral densities using finite-impulse-response filtering of white Gaussian noise (filter order $M = 1\times10^6$), then applied these to control pulse carriers in Qiskit-Dynamics simulations (tolerances $10^{-8}$, time step 83.3 ps) to compute qubit evolution and fidelity averaged over 20 noise realizations. Analytical decomposition of the noise-modulated carrier into double-sideband and residual amplitude modulation terms clarified the physical contributions.
result: Noise components at frequencies near the Rabi frequency (e.g., 10–20 MHz for 50–25 ns pulses) cause maximal fidelity loss, with components far from the carrier having negligible effect; for realistic oscillator spectra with $-60$ dBc/Hz at low offset and $-140$ dBc/Hz above 30 MHz, fidelities of 0.99998 (ten 150 ns pulses) and 0.997 (ten 150 ns pulses) were achieved, confirming that low-frequency and Rabi-resonant components dominate degradation.
